answer:
**Answer (natural-language hypothesis):** Among studies in the Psychology replication project (RPP) that successfully replicated (p ≤ 0.05, same-direction effect), the proportion whose replication team's most senior author was a junior professor (Assistant Professor) is **10 out of 35 = 28.6%** (95% Wilson CI: 16.3%–45.1%). Approximately **29% of replicated Psychology studies were led (by their most senior author) by a junior professor**. This proportion is sensitive to how "junior professor" is defined: counting both "Assistant Professor" and "Assistant" ranks gives 16/35 = 45.7%, and excluding the 4 drop-flagged replicated studies gives 10/31 = 32.3% (strict) or 16/31 = 51.6% (broad). The full seniority distribution of the 35 replicated studies' replication teams is: Assistant Professor 10 (28.6%), Professor 8 (22.9%), Associate Professor 7 (20.0%), Assistant 6 (17.1%), Researcher 4 (11.4%) — i.e., junior ranks collectively head a substantial share (~29–46%) of successfully replicated Psychology studies, and notably replication seniority data exists only for the Psychology project, making it the unique context for this question.

**Key assumptions stated explicitly:**
1. **rpp = Psychology**: "Psychology" maps to project == "rpp" per the data codebook; corroborated by Dataset 2 (which labels the same project "Psychology") and by rpp rows being exclusively Social/Cognitive discipline.
2. **seniority.r = replication-team seniority**: the codebook's description of seniority.r is a copy-error ("Most senior author in the original paper", identical to seniority.o); we read it, per the documented .o/.r convention, as the most senior author of the replication team.
3. **Denominator equivalence**: the denominator is all replicated studies in Psychology (n = 35); this is identical to the non-missing-seniority denominator because seniority.r has zero missingness among rpp studies.
4. **Junior professor = "Assistant Professor"** (headline, strict); the codebook distinguishes it from the separate "Assistant" category, so the broad definition is reported only as a labelled secondary figure.

**Workflow:** (1) loaded Dataset 1 (927×57); (2) confirmed project values and filtered to project == "rpp" (97 studies; replicated: 62 no / 35 yes, 0 missing); (3) subset replicated == 1 (n = 35); (4) tabulated seniority.r (no missingness, so no NA handling needed); (5) computed strict proportion with Wilson 95% CI, broad definition, and drop==False sensitivity; (6) verified no duplicate-id issues affect rpp (97 unique ids; `replicated` is per O/R pair, and only ml1/ml3 have multi-lab ids). Dataset 2 was inspected and excluded — it contains effect sizes/p-values only, no seniority or author variables.
